Candice: Welcome back, Amy. I'm so glad you will be joining our team!
Amy: Thanks, I'm really looking forward to it. My experience at the soup kitchen really confirmed my belief that we need to think of others.
Candice: I thought it might. Well, the first step is to decide how you can contribute to our project. What skills can you offer us?
Amy : I'm a life coach, so I really excel at things like motivation, introspection and communication.

Candice: Sounds like you're a real people-person. Do you have any experience with event planning?
Amy: Well, I run my own business, of course, so I have a great deal of experience with planning, organization and delivering workshops and conferences.
Candice: That's precisely what we need. As I've told you in Lesotho we focus on health, homes and jobs, but here at home the focus is on fundraising.
Amy: How do you go about it?

Candice: Well, our traditional method is hosting benefits like auctions, golf tournaments and concerts. This year we are also going to branch out by attempting a few new drives. We are going to crowdfund a medical center, but we also want to promote the sale of what we call “ethical gifts”.
Amy: Wow, that's really ambitious. Exciting, but ambitious.
Candice: It is, but we believe that if we can get enough donors, we can make it happen. We believe that if we combine these strategies under the direction of one motivated individual, we can reach our targets.
Amy: And that's where I come in, I guess.
Candice: Exactly, I'd like to see you hosting your first event as early as next month.

Linking is very common in natural conversation. Linking happens when certain sounds are connected. This happens between function words and content words. It also happens particularly when there is a consonant at the end of one word and a vowel at the beginning of the next.

Just a moment ...
You pronounce this as: Justa moment.

This consonant-vowel linking pattern can also link three or more words together.
For example:

My dog is a ...
You pronounce this as: My dogiza ...
Read these sentences aloud slowly and then more quickly, focusing on linking the consonant and vowel sounds together.
Well, the first step is to decide how you can contribute to our project.
But here at home the focus is on fundraising.

Intonation is the rise and fall of your voice. There are definite and expected intonation patterns in English.  The more you practice listening to and saying the correct intonation patterns, the better you will understand and be understood.

When you say items in a list, use a rising intonation for all the items in the list except for the last item. Use a falling intonation for the last item. Falling intonation indicates the end of the list.
I like bananas ⤴, apples ⤴, pears ⤴ and grapes ⤵.
Rising intonation tells your listener that you are not finished, and that there are other items in the list.
